name: Rate Limiter
tagline: Protect an API from abuse: from a single counter to a distributed token bucket
summary: A rate limiter decides, for every request, whether a client has exceeded its allowance and answers 429 when it has. The first version is a dictionary of counters and takes ten minutes to write. It becomes a real distributed-systems problem as soon as there is more than one server: counters must be shared, the decision must be atomic under concurrency, the check must cost almost nothing on the hot path, and the store it depends on will eventually be unavailable. Each step below keeps the previous design and changes only what the new scale or requirement demands, and the algorithm choice — fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter, token bucket, leaky bucket — is explained where it matters.
requirements: Limit requests per client key (API key, user id or IP) to N per time window; excess requests get HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
The limit decision adds well under 5 ms at p99 to every request.
Limits are enforced consistently across all API servers — spreading requests over servers must not multiply a client's allowance.
Rules (limits per endpoint, per client tier) are configurable and take effect without redeploying services.
Short bursts above the average rate are tolerated up to a defined size; sustained overuse is not.
Behaviour when the limiter's store is unavailable is an explicit policy (fail-open or fail-closed), not an accident.
Operators can see rejected requests per client and endpoint and get alerted when clients approach their limits.

steps.title: Single server with an in-memory fixed window
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. Without any limit one client running a retry loop can consume the whole server, so the goal is the simplest correct limiter: a counter per client per minute inside the API process.
steps.why: The fixed window algorithm keeps one integer per (client, window) pair: the key is the client id plus the current minute (e.g. user:42:2026-09-09T10:15), each request increments it, and the request is rejected when the counter exceeds N. It is O(1) memory per client, trivially fast because nothing leaves the process, and needs no extra infrastructure — the right call for one server. Its known flaw is the window boundary: a client may send N requests at 10:15:59 and another N at 10:16:00, so the true rate over any 60-second span can reach 2N. We accept that here because the cost of anything better is not justified by a single process; the next steps fix it when it starts to matter. Counters also vanish on restart, which is harmless at this scale.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Identified by API key or IP; every request carries the key the limiter counts against.

nodes.label: API Server
nodes.why: A middleware runs before the handler: increment the counter for (key, current minute), return 429 if it exceeds N, otherwise continue.

nodes.label: In-memory counters
nodes.why: A hash map inside the process: key → count. Entries for past minutes are evicted lazily so memory stays proportional to active clients.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Unrelated to limiting; shown because the limiter exists to protect it and the handlers in front of it.

steps.title: Shared counters in Redis
steps.problem: Running several API servers behind a load balancer broke the limit: each process kept its own map, so a client spreading requests across five servers got five times its allowance, and every deploy reset every counter to zero. The counter must live somewhere all servers can see.
steps.why: Moving the fixed-window counter into Redis gives every server the same view of every client. INCR is atomic on the server side and returns the new value, so two servers incrementing the same key at the same moment can never both observe a count below the limit and both admit — the classic race a read-then-write against a database would have. The key expires with EXPIRE set to the window length, so old windows clean themselves up and memory stays bounded. Redis is chosen over PostgreSQL because a limiter check runs on every request and must be sub-millisecond; a relational database would double the load it is supposed to protect. Memcached could hold the counters too but lacks the atomic scripting the next step needs. The costs: one network round-trip per request (typically 0.3–1 ms in the same zone), and Redis becomes a dependency for every request — so we decide the failure policy now: if Redis is unreachable we fail open (admit the request and log), because protecting availability of the API matters more than strictly enforcing quotas for a few seconds. The window-boundary burst from step 1 is still present.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged; sees one hostname.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Spreads a single client's requests over all servers, which is exactly why per-process counters stopped working.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Runs INCR on key:minute in Redis and sets EXPIRE on the first hit; admits if the returned count ≤ N.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Identical logic; because the count is shared, adding servers no longer multiplies the allowance.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Atomic INCR removes the check-then-act race; per-key TTL equal to the window length bounds memory.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Protected by the limiter; never consulted for the limit decision.

steps.title: Token bucket in an atomic Lua script
steps.problem: Two things broke. Clients discovered the window edge: bots timed 2N requests around the minute boundary and dashboards showed spikes the limit was supposed to prevent. And the two-command INCR-then-EXPIRE sequence had a gap — if a server crashed between them the key lived forever, and under high concurrency EXPIRE was occasionally applied to a key another server had already reset. The algorithm and its atomicity both need fixing.
steps.why: The options, in order of memory cost: (1) Sliding log — store every request timestamp in a sorted set, drop those older than the window, count the rest. Exact over any interval, but O(requests) memory per client, which is unaffordable at high limits. (2) Sliding window counter — keep the current and previous fixed-window counts and estimate the rate as current + previous × (fraction of the previous window still inside the sliding interval). Two integers per client, smooths the boundary spike, but it is an approximation that assumes traffic was evenly spread in the previous window. (3) Token bucket — each client has a bucket of capacity B that refills at R tokens per second; a request takes one token and is rejected if the bucket is empty. Two fields per client (tokens, last refill timestamp), allows bursts up to B while holding the long-run rate at R, and the burst size is a tunable product requirement rather than an accident of the clock. (4) Leaky bucket — requests enter a queue that drains at a constant rate; it smooths output perfectly but delays requests rather than rejecting them, which suits traffic shaping more than an API quota. We choose the token bucket: it directly expresses 'bursts of B, average R', which is what the requirements ask for, and costs the same as the sliding window counter. Atomicity is solved by putting the whole read-refill-decide-write sequence into one Lua script executed with EVALSHA; Redis runs scripts single-threaded, so no interleaving is possible and no lock is needed. Rules move out of code into a small table (limits per endpoint, per tier) that servers reload periodically, so a product change is a row update, not a deploy. The cost is that the script is now critical code that must be tested carefully, and clock skew between servers is avoided by taking the timestamp from Redis TIME inside the script rather than from the caller.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Now receives X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers so well-behaved clients can back off.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Sends the client key, capacity and refill rate (looked up from cached rules) to the script and gets back allow/deny plus remaining tokens in one round-trip.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Same script, same rules; no server-local state is involved in the decision.

nodes.label: Redis (Lua)
nodes.why: One hash per client (tokens, last_refill). The script refills by elapsed time, decrements, writes back and sets TTL — all in one atomic step using Redis's own clock.

nodes.label: Rules Table
nodes.why: Small, rarely changed table read every few seconds by servers; changing a limit is a row update, not a deploy.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Protected; unchanged.

steps.title: Limiting at the API gateway with local and global buckets
steps.problem: The limiter is now copy-pasted into every service in several languages, and each copy drifts. The single Redis is the hottest component in the system because every request in every service pays a round-trip to it, and when it slows down every service slows with it. A second region made it worse: cross-region round-trips to one Redis add tens of milliseconds, violating the latency budget.
steps.why: Limiting moves out of the services and into the API gateway, the single entry point every request already passes through. That gives one implementation, one place to change rules, and 429s that never reach a service. To take Redis off the hot path we split the bucket in two tiers. Each gateway node keeps a local token bucket per client in memory and decides most requests from it with no network call; every 100 ms or every K requests it reconciles with the global bucket in Redis, requesting a batch of tokens and learning how much the client has consumed through other gateway nodes. The global view is therefore approximate by at most one reconciliation interval, which is an acceptable overshoot for quotas measured in requests per minute, and the p99 cost of the decision drops to microseconds. Redis itself becomes a cluster sharded by client key so no single node holds all counters, deployed per region with global buckets keyed by region for the strict per-region limits and a cheaper, eventually consistent sum for the account-wide ones. A circuit breaker around the reconciliation call makes the fail-open policy from step 2 explicit: if Redis is unreachable the gateway keeps enforcing from its local bucket alone, which degrades to 'N per gateway node' rather than to no limit at all. The costs are a smarter gateway that must be operated as a critical tier, an approximation that determined attackers can exploit for a few hundred milliseconds, and more moving parts in the failure-mode story.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Routed to the nearest region by DNS; sees the same limits everywhere.

nodes.label: API Gateway A
nodes.why: Decides most requests from an in-memory bucket per client; only reconciles with Redis in batches.

nodes.label: API Gateway B
nodes.why: Another gateway node; its local view of a client can differ from A's by at most one reconciliation interval.

nodes.label: Redis Cluster
nodes.why: Holds the authoritative bucket per client; gateways request token batches with the same Lua script, so hot keys are spread across shards.

nodes.label: Circuit Breaker
nodes.why: If reconciliation to Redis fails or slows, the gateway trips the breaker and enforces from local buckets only instead of blocking or admitting everything.

nodes.label: Rules Service
nodes.why: Serves the rules table from step 3 to gateways and pushes changes so a new limit is live in seconds.

nodes.label: Orders Service
nodes.why: No limiter code of its own anymore; trusts that the gateway already admitted the request.

nodes.label: Search Service
nodes.why: Same: per-endpoint limits are expressed as gateway rules, not service code.

nodes.label: Databases
nodes.why: Protected; the gateway ensures excess traffic never reaches them.

steps.title: Per-tenant tiers, live rules and analytics
steps.scale: Enterprise customers · billions of requests per day
steps.problem: One limit for everyone stopped fitting the business: paying customers need higher quotas and separate limits per endpoint, support cannot answer 'why was I throttled at 14:02', and abuse is only discovered when a backend falls over. The limiter works but is a black box to operators and to customers.
steps.why: Three additions turn the limiter into a product feature. First, rules become tiered: a tenant maps to a plan, a plan maps to buckets per endpoint group (e.g. reads 1,000/min, writes 100/min, exports 10/min), and the rules service publishes changes over Redis Pub/Sub so every gateway hot-reloads them within a second — no polling, no deploy. Second, every decision (allow or deny, tenant, endpoint, remaining tokens) is emitted as an event to Kafka from the gateway asynchronously, so the hot path pays only an in-memory append. An analytics consumer aggregates the stream into a search index for support dashboards and per-customer usage pages, and a second consumer detects anomalies such as a tenant hitting 100% of its quota across many keys, which usually means leaked credentials. Third, Prometheus scrapes the gateways for rejection counts and near-limit ratios, giving operators alerts before customers complain and giving sales a signal about who needs a bigger plan. Responses carry standard headers (RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After) so clients can self-regulate. The costs are substantial: Kafka and a search cluster are heavy components to operate for what began as a hash map, the event volume equals the request volume so retention must be short with aggregates kept long, and tiered rules make the configuration itself something that needs review and versioning.

nodes.label: Tenant Client
nodes.why: Receives RateLimit-* headers; enterprise tenants see the quotas of their tier.

nodes.label: API Gateway Fleet
nodes.why: Applies the tenant's plan rules from steps 3–4 and appends each decision to an in-memory buffer flushed to Kafka.

nodes.label: Redis Cluster
nodes.why: Still the authoritative bucket store; additionally carries rule-change notifications so gateways reload instantly.

nodes.label: Rules Service
nodes.why: Owns the tenant/plan/limit model in PostgreSQL and publishes changes; an admin UI edits it with review and version history.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Absorbs one small event per request without touching the hot path; partitioned by tenant so consumers can aggregate per customer in order.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Relational fit: a tenant has a plan, a plan has many limits, changes are audited.

nodes.label: Analytics Consumer
nodes.why: Aggregates decisions per tenant/endpoint/minute into a search index for support and customer usage pages, and flags anomalous quota exhaustion.

nodes.label: Prometheus
nodes.why: Scrapes gateway metrics; alert rules fire when a tenant sustains >80% of quota or when reject ratio jumps fleet-wide.

nodes.label: Backend Services
nodes.why: Receive only admitted traffic, sized for the sum of paid quotas rather than for worst-case abuse.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show a rate limiter growing. Step 1: a client calls one API server whose middleware increments an in-memory fixed-window counter before touching PostgreSQL. Step 2: a load balancer spreads requests over several API servers that share fixed-window counters in a single Redis using atomic INCR and EXPIRE. Step 3: the servers switch to a token-bucket algorithm executed as an atomic Lua script in Redis, with limits read from a small rules table. Step 4: limiting moves into API gateway nodes that keep local token buckets and reconcile in batches with a sharded Redis cluster behind a circuit breaker, while a rules service pushes configuration; backend services no longer contain limiter code. Step 5: gateways apply per-tenant tiered rules hot-reloaded via Redis Pub/Sub, emit every decision to Kafka for an analytics consumer that feeds dashboards and abuse detection, and expose metrics to Prometheus.
